question.problem: By the multiplicative property of congruences, ${21}^{4}≡$
question.worked_solution:
The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a≡b\,\text{and}\,c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
{21}^{4}=(3\cdot 7)^{4}={3}^{2}\cdot {3}^{2}\cdot {7}^{2}\cdot {7}^{2}.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡1\cdot 6+3\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡1\cdot 0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡3\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\ {7}^{2} & ≡49\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡8\cdot 6+1\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡8\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{21}^{4} & ≡{3}^{2}\cdot {3}^{2}\cdot {7}^{2}\cdot {7}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡3\cdot 3\cdot 1\cdot 1\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡1\cdot 6+3\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡1\cdot 0+3\, & (\text{mod}\,6) \\  & ≡3\, & (\text{mod}\,6)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{21}^{4}≡3\,\,(\text{mod}\,6).
$$
